answers: Suspension of the rules is the most commonly used procedure to call up measures on the floor of the House of Representatives. As the name suggests, the procedure allows the House to suspend its standing and statutory rules in order to consider broadly supported legislation in an expedited manner. More specifically, the House temporarily sets aside its rules that govern the raising and consideration of measures and assumes a new set of constraints particular to the suspension procedure. The suspension of the rules procedure has several parliamentary advantages: (1) it allows nonprivileged measures to be raised on the House floor without the need for a special rule, (2) it enables the consideration of measures that would otherwise be subject to a point of order, and (3) it streamlines floor action by limiting debate and prohibiting floor amendments. Given these features, as well as the required two-thirds supermajority vote for passage, suspension motions are generally used to process less controversial legislation. In the 114th Congress (2015-2016), measures considered under suspension made up 62% of the bills and resolutions that received floor action in the House (743 out of 1,200 measures). The majority of suspension measures were House bills (83%), followed by Senate bills (11%) and House resolutions (4%). The measures covered a variety of policy areas but most often addressed government operations, such as the designation of federal facilities or amending administrative policies. Most measures that are considered in the House under the suspension procedure are sponsored by a House or Senate majority party member. However, suspension is the most common House procedure used to consider minority-party-sponsored legislation regardless of whether the legislation originated in the House or Senate. In 2015 and 2016, minority-party members sponsored 31% of suspension measures, compared to 9% of legislation subject to different procedures, including privileged business (17 measures), unanimous consent (21 measures), and under the terms of a special rule (one Senate bill). Most suspension measures are referred to at least one House committee before their consideration on the floor. The House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform (now called the Committee on Oversight and Reform) was the committee of primary jurisdiction for the plurality of suspension measures considered in the 114th Congress. Additional committees—such as Energy and Commerce, Homeland Security, Natural Resources, Foreign Affairs, and Veterans' Affairs—also served as the primary committee for a large number of suspension measures. Suspension motions are debatable for up to 40 minutes. In most cases, only a fraction of that debate time is actually used. In the 114th Congress, the average amount of time spent considering a motion to suspend the rules was 13 minutes and 10 seconds. The House adopted nearly every suspension motion considered in 2015 and 2016. Approval by the House, however, did not guarantee final approval in the 114th Congress. The Senate passed or agreed to 40% of the bills, joint resolutions, and concurrent resolutions initially considered in the House under suspension of the rules, and 276 measures were signed into law. This report briefly describes the suspension of the rules procedure, which is defined in House Rule XV, and provides an analysis of measures considered under this procedure during the 114th Congress. Figures and one table display statistics on the use of the procedure, including the prevalence and form of suspension measures, sponsorship of measures by party, committee consideration, length of debate, voting, resolution of differences between the chambers, and the final status of legislation. In addition, an Appendix illustrates trends in the use of the suspension procedure from the 110th to the 114th Congress (2007-2016).

This procedure allows the House to expedite the consideration of nonprivileged legislation by waiving points of order, limiting debate to 40 minutes, and prohibiting floor amendments. It requires a two-thirds supermajority vote and is typically used for widely supported measures, such as government operations and facility designations, rather than complex or contentious legislation.

**Statistical Overview of the 114th Congress**
During the 114th Congress (2015–2016), suspension was the most common method for bringing measures to the floor. Of the 1,200 measures receiving floor action, 62% (743) were considered under suspension, compared to 14% under special rules. Most of these measures were bills (94%), with House bills comprising 83% of the total. The procedure is the primary vehicle for minority-sponsored legislation, accounting for 85% of such measures considered on the floor.

**Committee and Procedural Details**
Suspension motions are generally in order on Mondays, Tuesdays, and Wednesdays, though they can occur on other days via unanimous consent or special rules. Debate is managed by two floor managers who control 20 minutes each. In practice, debate is often brief; the average consideration time was 13 minutes and 10 seconds, with half of the measures debated for 10 minutes or less. While the motion to suspend and pass the measure is a single vote, 28% of measures triggered a subsequent recorded vote.

**Legislative Outcomes**
The two-thirds threshold ensures high passage rates in the House. Of the 619 House bills initially considered under suspension, 612 passed. However, success in the Senate is less certain. Only 32% of House bills and 45% of House resolutions passed the Senate. Of the 703 measures that passed both chambers, 60 required a resolution of differences. Ultimately, 193 House bills, 82 Senate bills, and 1 joint resolution became public law during the 114th Congress.
